newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel's EMU budget focus shifts to German regions.
newsitem.headline: Waigel's EMU budget focus shifts to German regions.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel's campaign to get Germany fit next year for European monetary union (EMU) is set to open up a new front this week as he tries to get state and local governments to cut borrowing.

Waigel's federal spending plans cleared parliament's budget committee stage last week. The central government budget deficit will fall to 53.3 billion marks ($35.38 billion) in 1997 from 73 billion marks. But that is only part of the story.

He will need all of his famed tenacity at talks on Wednesday to browbeat state and local governments into cuts too, since under the Maastricht treaty it is the total public sector deficit that counts towards qualifying for EMU.

"We are talking about a lot of money, and recent years have shown that these talks are very difficult," Peter Pietsch, an economist at Commerzbank in Frankfurt, said. "With such radical cuts this year these talks are going to be even harder."

Waigel said last week Germany would beat the Maastricht deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product "by a sufficient safety margin" in 1997, the year in which countries will have to prove their readiness for monetary union in 1999.
A Finance Ministry paper, details of which were published on Monday by the Handelsblatt financial daily, sketches out how cuts in the German deficit could be carved out.

Germany's 16 states are expected to reduce their deficits to a combined 36 billion marks next year from 44 billion marks this year. Meanwhile local government new borrowing should fall to seven billion marks from nine billion marks.

Taking into account other factors, the total public sector deficit would come out at 99 billion marks -- down 20 billion marks on this year -- and equivalent to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
But Germany would still just miss the treaty's target for state debt of 60 percent of GDP, with total borrowing rising to 61 percent of GDP in 1997, Handelsblatt said.

This week's talks are likely to be tricky because the Social Democratic (SPD) opposition rules in most German states. It has already done its best to mangle Waigel's tax plans through its blocking majority in the upper house of parliament.

Local leaders are also up in arms, complaining that changes made under the centre-right coalition government's austerity package mean they will lose out on tax revenues and funding for job creation schemes.
Rudolf Scharping, SPD parliamentary head, called on Monday for Waigel to lighten the burden on the communes.
"It is not acceptable that Waigel fixes federal finances at the cost of local governments," Scharping, flanked by several SPD city mayors, told a news conference.
Whether the real numbers will turn out as the Finance Ministry foresees is unclear, because Waigel has no sanctions to enforce financial discipline at state or local level.
That has led Waigel to call for an internal German "stability pact" to secure lasting fiscal prudence, matching his drive for tough fines against EMU states whose financial discipline lapses.
